question: Q54
question_text: Is there a checked Canadian Indigenous critique, before 2000, of fur-trade and native–newcomer historiography?
short_answer: Yes. The clearest checked case is Winona Stevenson (now Winona Wheeler), 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories, Part I: The Othering of Indigenous History', Saskatchewan History 50, no. 2 (Fall 1998): 24–27, read in full. It names 'Indian–White Relations' historians and argues that, by relying on the records left by one side of the relationship, even agency-centred work keeps the story 'within the colonialist framework' and 'others' Indigenous oral history. LaRocque's 1999 dissertation, already an atlas source, is the second checked case: passages now read criticise the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk, and fur-trade historians' double standards. Sioui (1989) is a checked critique of conventional history in general, including its focus on change in material culture. Adams (1975) critiques official and school history rather than this academic field. Dickason writes corrective history, not historiographical critique. Trigger, Kelm and Brownlie are non-Indigenous context.

method.verification: Each source was checked against a record: Crossref (mailto=jic823@usask.ca), OpenAlex, iPortal (USask), Érudit, MSpace (Manitoba), publisher and catalogue pages, Manitoba Historical Society. Where the full text was read, the passages are noted. Project MUSE blocked automated reading of the Kelm–Brownlie pieces, so their argument comes from how strict PhDs in the corpus characterise it.
method.citation_counts: Strict History PhDs: Dissertation nodes with in_analysis, years 2009–2026 (N=1,303; 179 at francophone universities). Counted by dissertation, not by citation. Francophone = montreal, uqam, laval, sherbrooke. Script: answers/research/q54_counts.py. Works are pooled across title variants by surname-prefixed work id plus a title regex. Author totals pool person keys and are not authority-reviewed.

candidates.candidate: Winona Wheeler (published before c. 2000 as Winona Stevenson)
candidates.atlas_status: In the atlas only as a contributor to Indigenous history, through Leddy (2010); her own works are not atlas sources.
candidates.author_self_description: The author note in the 1998 article (p. 24) says: 'She is Cree (Assiniboine, Saulteaux, and Irish) and a member of the Fisher River Cree First Nation, Koostatak, Manitoba.' At the time she was Head of the Indian Studies Department, Saskatchewan Indian Federated College. The source states this; it is not inferred here.

works.citation: Winona Stevenson, 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories, Part I: The Othering of Indigenous History', Saskatchewan History 50, no. 2 (Fall 1998): 24–27.

verification.note: The open-access PDF of the whole issue is a scan. I ran OCR on the article pages (journal pp. 24–27, PDF pp. 26–29) and read them in full. Note that the year is 1998 (Fall), not 1999.

works.argument: Addresses 'Historians of Indian–White Relations' (p. 24). Argues that 'The concept "Indian–White Relations" presupposes at least two parties' (p. 24), and that 'By focusing on the historical remnants left by one side of that relationship, historians reinforce the colonialist notion that Western historical canons and conventions are superior' (p. 25). It acknowledges the recent 'outpouring' of work by Indian–White relations historians and 'New Indian Historians', and work that celebrates Indigenous peoples 'as active agents in encounter with Europeans'; its notes cite Carter 1990, Pettipas 1994, Tough 1996, Ray 1996 and Peers 1994 as examples. It then argues that 'their continued dependence on documents maintains the academic tradition of telling the stories of my peoples' historical experiences within the colonialist framework' (p. 25). It contrasts Rankean source canons with Cree oral-historical practice, using the example of keeping the memory of Treaty 6. Its purpose: 'to encourage historians to engage in some self-reflection about their own attitudes and treatment of Indigenous oral histories' (p. 24).
works.scope_fit: Direct. Explicitly about Canadian 'Indian–White Relations' historiography and its archival base, including the agency turn. Prairie and treaty focus rather than fur trade as such, though its examples include fur-trade and economic history (Ray, Tough, Peers).

works.citation: Winona Stevenson, 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories, Part 3: The Social Relations of Oral History', Saskatchewan History 51 (1999).

verification.note: Known only from the graph's bibliography record (container Saskatchewan History, 1999) and a web-search summary giving 51, no. 1 (1999): 29–35; one search summary gave issue 2. No catalogue record was opened. Do not cite yet.

works.citation: Winona Wheeler [Stevenson], 'Calling Badger and the Symbols of the Spirit Languages: The Cree Origins of the Syllabic System', Oral History Forum 19–20 (1999–2000): 19–24.

verification.note: I read the USask Gladue database record and its abstract. The record's page range ('19-4') is garbled; 19–24 comes from a search summary. Body not read.

works.argument: From the abstract: the article challenges 'the unchallenged myth which has persisted over 160 years' that missionary James Evans originated Cree syllabics. Because Cree people were not consulted, their oral histories were ignored, and the 'European/colonial account dominates discourse'.
works.scope_fit: Partial. A critique of one missionary-history claim and of document-only method, not of the field as a whole.

works.citation: Winona Stevenson, '"Ethnic" Assimilates "Indigenous": A Study in Intellectual Neocolonialism', Wicazo Sa Review 13, no. 1 (1998): 33–51.

verification.note: Crossref metadata checked. The OpenAlex abstract (opening text) was read. End page 51 is not confirmed (Crossref gives first page 33 only).

works.argument: Argues that Native Studies should not be housed under Ethnic Studies, because doing so produces unbalanced power relations and the marginalising and silencing of Native people (paper given at UBC in 1994).
works.scope_fit: No. A critique of how the academy organises Native Studies, not of fur-trade or native–newcomer historiography. Its existence also corrects the draft's statement that Crossref found nothing for her.

works.citation: Winona Stevenson, 'Decolonizing Tribal Histories' (PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley, 2000).

verification.note: A web-search summary of her USask profile lists it, but the profile page opened empty. No ProQuest or Berkeley record was opened.

author_citation_graph.caveat: Includes 'Gender, Race and Policy: Aboriginal Women and the State in Canada and Australia' (1996, keyed to McGrath; 3 PhDs), a co-authorship that was not checked here.

candidates.assessment: The strongest candidate. Before 2000, a Canadian, self-identified Cree historian wrote an explicit, checked critique of 'Indian–White Relations' historiography and of the agency turn's continued dependence on documents. The dissertation corpus barely cites it: Part I appears in 0 strict PhDs, and her 1998–99 essays in 1–2 each.

candidates.atlas_status: In the atlas as a critic in Indigenous history; source ind126_larocque_thesis (p. 34 read).
candidates.author_self_description: In the dissertation (PDF p. 30): 'As a Nehiyawewsquoh (Cree speaking Native woman) I have a dialectical relationship with colonial...' (the line continues beyond the passage read).

works.citation: Emma LaRocque, Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices in Canadian Historiography and Literature (PhD dissertation, University of Manitoba, 1999).

verification.note: Abstract checked on MSpace. The PDF was downloaded and passages read; page references are PDF pages of NQ45006.pdf, not the printed numbers.

works.argument: The abstract frames Native writers' resistance to misrepresentation in Canadian historiography through a 'civilization–savagery' framework. Passages bearing on this field: (a) PDF p. 249 criticises 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s–1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)'. It calls this 'a much improved approach to Native history' than earlier racist material, but says its ethnological description has a 'distancing' effect and 'results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable'; the footnote uses Van Kirk's Many Tender Ties as an example. (b) PDF p. 102: 'It is quite common, for example, for fur trade historians to generalize Indians as having a "covetous disposition"', a double standard. (c) PDF p. 109: 'fur trade historian E.E. Rich persistently uses colonial phrases such as "crafty"...'. (d) PDF p. 30, note: Trigger's 'The Historians' Indian' is called 'an astonishingly optimistic view of French historiography'. (e) PDF p. 135: Trigger's foreword to Sioui's For an Amerindian Autohistory is 'a typical example of containment'.
works.scope_fit: Direct, and it names fur-trade and native–newcomer historians. Its main object is broader: representation in historiography and literature.

verification.note: Atlas source ind126_larocque_book. A critique of stereotypes in curricula, not of the academic field.

author_citation_graph.caveat: The P:laroque|emma key includes one misattributed record (Walz, 'Three Views of Riel').

candidates.assessment: A checked, explicit critique from 1999 that names Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk as well as fur-trade historians. It is already an atlas source; the draft's wording can now rest on read pages rather than on p. 34 alone.

candidates.atlas_status: In the atlas; sources ind126_sioui_interview and ind126_sioui_english.
candidates.author_self_description: 'Je suis un Huron-Wendat traditionnel ... Je suis historien de profession' (Québec français 80, 1991, p. 76).

works.citation: Georges E. Sioui, Pour une autohistoire amérindienne: essai sur les fondements d'une morale sociale (Québec: Presses de l'Université Laval, 1989); English translation For an Amerindian Autohistory (McGill-Queen's University Press, 1992), translated by Sheila Fischman, with a foreword by Bruce Trigger.

verification.note: I re-read the 1991 interview (Yolande Ricard, Québec français 80: 76–78), PDF text extracted. The MQUP page now redirects and returns 404. The Trigger foreword is attested by LaRocque 1999 (PDF p. 135).

works.argument: In the interview Sioui explains 'autohistoire' as the idea 'qu'il n'a pas encore existé d'histoire véritable des Amérindiens, puisque l'histoire conventionnelle n'a pas encore inventé de méthode qui permette d'intégrer la vision amérindienne à son discours'. He says he is not interested in changes in material culture ('Je me désintéresse de tout l'aspect des changements dans la culture matérielle') and denounces 'les mythes euro-américains de la disparition de l'amérindien, ainsi que celui de l'évolutionnisme culturel' (p. 77).
works.scope_fit: Direct but general. Its target is conventional Euro-American history and the acculturation and disappearance framings that structured New France and Wendat encounter history. It does not name fur-trade historians in the passage read.

works.citation: Georges E. Sioui, Les Wendats: une civilisation méconnue (Presses de l'Université Laval, 1994); revised English edition Huron-Wendat: The Heritage of the Circle, trans. Jane Brierley (UBC Press, 1999).

verification.note: I checked the catalogue record (1999 revised edition, translator, publisher). The jacket description and the Steckley review (CBRA) are known only from a web-search summary; the CBRA page returned 403.

works.scope_fit: Possibly a counter-history to the Huronia and dispersal literature, but no checked text says it criticises particular historians.

candidates.assessment: Keep as already drafted. It is a checked pre-2000 critique of conventional history's method, more general than the native–newcomer field. Note the francophone pattern: the autohistory is cited by 0 francophone strict PhDs, and Sioui's work overall by 2.

candidates.atlas_status: In the atlas as a historian in Indigenous history (source ind126_adams).

works.citation: Howard Adams, Prison of Grass: Canada from the Native Point of View (Toronto: New Press, 1975; revised ed., Saskatoon: Fifth House, 1989).

verification.note: Read the Connexions catalogue description of the 1989 revised edition. The 1975 New Press imprint is from a WorldCat result (page returned 403). The atlas's USask encyclopedia record was reused. Book body not read; one passage is known through LaRocque 1999 (PDF p. 209, her reading of Prison of Grass p. 18).

works.argument: The publisher's description says Adams 'contrasts the official history found in the federal government's documents' with 'the unpublished history of the Indian and Métis people', and calls the book 'a classic of revisionist history'. LaRocque (1999) reports that Adams quotes a 1970s Saskatchewan elementary textbook that portrays Indians as warlike scalpers, and rebuts it.
works.scope_fit: A critique of official, national and school history from a Métis and anticolonial position. It predates most of the academic native–newcomer field (Ray 1974, Van Kirk and Brown 1980), so it cannot be a critique of that field. Cite it as an antecedent Indigenous counter-history, not as the critique of this entry's literature.

candidates.assessment: Do not present it as a critique of fur-trade or native–newcomer historiography. Mention it at most as an earlier Indigenous counter-narrative to official history. It is the most cited of the Indigenous candidates (17 strict PhDs, none francophone).

candidates.atlas_status: In the atlas, and on the native_newcomer draft roster as a member of the field.

works.citation: Olive Patricia Dickason, Canada's First Nations: A History of Founding Peoples from Earliest Times (Toronto: McClelland & Stewart, 1992).

verification.note: Read Frieda Esau Klippenstein's review, Manitoba History 25 (Spring 1993). Publisher not re-checked here (the atlas has ind126_dickason_survey).

works.argument: According to the reviewer, the book 'differs from previous writings more in point of view than in sources', and its sources and methods place it 'in the mainstream of academic scholarship'. A central theme is that Amerindians and Inuit are 'in the truest sense Canada's "founding nations"'.
works.scope_fit: A corrective synthesis written within the field's methods, not a critique of the historiography.

verification.note: Atlas ind126_dickason_myth (publisher description). It studies sixteenth-century European ideas of savagery, not modern historiography.

works.citation: Bruce G. Trigger, 'The Historians' Indian: Native Americans in Canadian Historical Writing from Charlevoix to the Present', Canadian Historical Review 67, no. 3 (1986): 315–342.

verification.note: Crossref metadata and the OpenAlex abstract (opening paragraph) were read. Reprinted in The Contested Past (2002), DOI 10.3138/9781442680906-060.

works.argument: A survey of how Native peoples have been treated in Canadian historical writing. It relates 'successive fashions in the historical portrayal of native peoples to changing anthropological understanding', and notes 'a new concern to integrate the findings of ethnohistorians into the broader framework of national history'.
works.scope_fit: Reflexive historiography from within the field. LaRocque (1999) called it 'astonishingly optimistic' about French historiography.

candidates.candidate: Mary-Ellen Kelm and Robin Jarvis Brownlie, 1994 debate (not Indigenous; context)

works.citation: Robin Brownlie and Mary-Ellen Kelm, 'Desperately Seeking Absolution: Native Agency as Colonialist Alibi?', Canadian Historical Review 75, no. 4 (December 1994): 543–556 (Notes and Comments).

verification.note: OpenAlex gives volume 75, issue 4, pp. 543–556, with the Project MUSE landing page. MUSE served a bot challenge, so the body was not read. Crossref has no record. The argument is taken from strict PhDs in the corpus: Crystal Gail Fraser (Alberta 2019) writes that Kelm and Brownlie 'cautioned historians against using the concept of Indigenous agency, since most analyses tended to deny lived trauma and overlooked the responsibility of settlers'. Cathleen Clark (Toronto 2023) quotes their phrase 'insidious tendency to turn Native agency into colonialist alibi'.

works.argument: (Secondary characterisation.) The stress on Native agency in recent native–newcomer history could minimise colonial harm and absolve colonisers.
works.scope_fit: Direct, and internal to the field; the authors are not Indigenous.

works.citation: Douglas Cole, J.R. Miller and Mary-Ellen Kelm [with Robin Brownlie], 'Notes and Comments: Desperately Seeking Absolution: Responses and a Reply', Canadian Historical Review 76, no. 4 (1995): 628–642.

verification.note: OpenAlex lists the authors as Cole, Miller, Kelm, Trottier, Greer and Wien. The last three probably come from adjacent items and are not adopted. Volume, issue and pages come from corpus bibliographies (Waterloo 2025: 76, no. 4, 628–642), not from a publisher record. This resolves the draft's 'Cole' note: the graph records keyed to Cole are the 1995 responses.

candidates.assessment: Context only. A pre-2000 critique from inside the field, not an Indigenous critique. The draft describes it correctly; it can now cite pages and the 1995 exchange.

corpus_note: Of 1,303 strict PhDs (2009–2026), 28 cite at least one pre-2000 Indigenous-authored critique or counter-history in this set: Adams 1975, Sioui 1989/1992, LaRocque 1975/1996/1999, and Stevenson/Wheeler 1998–99. Only 2 of the 28 are at francophone universities. Just 3 of them also cite Kelm and Brownlie 1994, and 1 cites Trigger's 'The Historians' Indian'. The Indigenous critiques reach the corpus mainly through Adams (17), and later through LaRocque's When the Other Is Me (2010; 8).

proposed_source_record.citation: Winona Stevenson [Wheeler], 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories, Part I: The Othering of Indigenous History', Saskatchewan History 50, no. 2 (Fall 1998): 24–27.

verification.note: Open-access issue PDF (scan) read in full via OCR, pp. 24–27. Argues that 'Indian–White Relations' historians, by relying on the remnants left by one side, keep even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and 'other' Indigenous oral histories. The author note states that she is Cree and a member of Fisher River Cree First Nation.

recommendation.suggested_description_sentence: Indigenous scholars questioned the framing itself. Sioui (1989) argued that conventional history had no method for Indigenous self-interpretation. Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on the records of one side, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside. LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still distanced and ‘othered’ the people it studied.
recommendation.suggested_strand_focus: Sioui (1989), Stevenson/Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) criticise the relations framing from Indigenous standpoints. Their targets are its reliance on colonial documents, its disregard of oral history and its ethnological distance. Adams (1975) is an earlier counter-history of official and school history, not of this field.
cautions: Date Stevenson Part I to Fall 1998, not 1999.
Do not say 'the first' Indigenous critique.
Attribute identity only to the source's own author note; the atlas records no identity classification.
Do not cite Part III (1999) or the 2000 Berkeley dissertation until they are checked.
Kelm and Brownlie's argument is still from secondary characterisations; phrase it as a question ('asked whether...'), as the draft already does.
